passage: Dear Kamal, I'm writing this because every time I try to talk, one of us walks away. For months you've been in your room with the door shut. You snap at me when I ask about school. On Sunday I shouted, "Just cheer up, what's wrong with you?" I'm sorry. I was frightened, and it came out as anger. I've been reading, and talking to your class teacher. I think you might be carrying something heavy, and that is not your fault. I'm not going to lecture you. I'd like to listen, whenever you're ready, even if it's just to sit together. I've also booked an appointment with a counsellor for Thursday. Will you come with me? I'll wait in the car if you want. I love you, stubborn boy. Amma (Urmila)

qa.q: When is the counsellor appointment?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when 'Just cheer up' came out as a shout?
qa.a: Urmila felt frightened, and the fear came out as anger.

qa.q: What change in approach does Urmila offer Kamal?
qa.a: Urmila apologises, promises to listen instead of lecture, and has arranged professional support with the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel reading this letter compared with being shouted at?
qa.a: Kamal may feel less blamed and more cared for, which could make Kamal more willing to talk or go on Thursday.

grounding: It shows a parent who sees a teen pull away and snap, feels frightened and angry, and turns to concern, listening and professional support instead of telling the teen to cheer up.

passage: "You want to know how it started, Anand? I'm Bhupen, and I'll tell you straight. I was angry. My son Tushar was fifteen. Overnight, it felt like, he stopped talking to us. Door shut. Plate left full. If I asked about cricket, which he'd loved, he snapped, 'Leave me alone!' I thought, this boy is being rude to his own father. I shouted back more than once. I felt helpless, and helpless turned into angry. Then my wife showed me his notebook, full of 'I'm tired' written over and over. That stopped me cold. That night I knocked, sat on the floor by his bed and said, 'I'm not angry. I'm worried about you. Tell me when you can.' He didn't talk much. But the next week he let me take him to a counsellor. We're still going, together."

qa.q: What was written over and over in Tushar's notebook?
qa.a: I'm tired.

qa.q: What made Bhupen feel angry at first?
qa.a: He felt helpless when his son pulled away and snapped, and the helplessness turned into anger.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Bhupen approached his son?
qa.a: Seeing the notebook, he knocked, sat on the floor and spoke with worry instead of blame, then took him to a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Tushar have experienced his father's shouting before the change?
qa.a: He may have felt more alone and misunderstood, pushing him further behind the shut door.

grounding: A father recalls feeling helpless and angry as his son pulled away and snapped, then approaching with concern, listening and arranging professional support.

passage: In their flat in Lima, Hiroshi heard the door slam again. For two months Diego, fifteen, had barely spoken at dinner, quit the football team and snapped at the smallest question. That night Hiroshi lost his temper. "Enough! Just cheer up and stop sulking!" Diego stared at him and walked out. Hiroshi sat alone, angry and then helpless, his hands shaking. After an hour he knocked. "I'm sorry I shouted. I'm not angry with you. I'm worried." Silence. He sat on the floor outside the door. "I'll just stay here." After a long while, Diego opened the door and sat beside him. He didn't say much. But the next morning Hiroshi called the school counsellor, and they booked an appointment together.

qa.q: What team did Diego quit?
qa.a: He quit the football team.

qa.q: How did Hiroshi feel after Diego walked out?
qa.a: He felt angry and then helpless, sitting alone with his hands shaking.

qa.q: What worked better than telling Diego to cheer up?
qa.a: Apologising, saying he was worried rather than angry, staying close and then arranging professional support with the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Diego have felt when his father sat outside his door?
qa.a: Diego may have felt less alone and more cared for, which is why he eventually opened the door and sat beside him.

grounding: Shows a parent feeling angry and helpless as his son withdraws, who moves from blame to concern, listens and arranges professional support.

passage: In the school counsellor's office, Rashmi sat stiffly, handbag on her knees. "Pihu is just rude now. She shouts at me, locks her door, won't eat with us. I'm tired of it." Vandana, the counsellor, nodded. "That sounds exhausting. Can I tell you what Pihu's teachers see? She's gone very quiet in class, stopped art club and sits alone." Rashmi's face changed. "She loved art." "Sometimes when teenagers pull away and snap, it's a sign they're struggling, not attitude. What if tonight you just say you're worried and listen?" That evening Rashmi knocked, sat on the edge of Pihu's bed and said, "I'm worried about you, not angry." Pihu cried for a long time. The next day Rashmi booked the doctor's appointment Vandana had suggested.

qa.q: What club did Pihu stop going to?
qa.a: She stopped going to art club.

qa.q: How was Rashmi feeling when she first sat in the office?
qa.a: She felt tired and angry, seeing Pihu's behaviour only as rudeness.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi approach Pihu differently?
qa.a: The counsellor shared what teachers saw and suggested speaking with concern, not blame, so Rashmi said she was worried, listened and then booked a doctor.

qa.q: How might Pihu have felt when her mother said she was worried, not angry?
qa.a: Pihu may have felt relieved and finally safe enough to let her sadness out, which is why she cried.

grounding: Shows a parent who first feels angry at her withdrawn, snapping daughter, then approaches with concern, listens and arranges professional support.

passage:
Sharmila,
I'm writing this because when I try to talk, we both end up shouting.
For weeks I've watched you stop eating with us, stop calling your friends, stay in your room with the lights off. When you snapped at me on Sunday, I snapped back and told you to "just cheer up." That was wrong. I was frightened and I felt helpless, and it came out as anger. I'm sorry.
I'm not angry with you. I'm worried, and I love you.
I don't want to fix you with a lecture. I want to listen, whenever you're ready. I've also made an appointment with Dr Lobo for Thursday, to talk about how you've been feeling. I'll come with you, or wait outside, whatever you prefer.
Your Mumma, Simran

qa.q: When is the appointment with Dr Lobo?
qa.a: The appointment is on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when snapping back on Sunday?
qa.a: Simran felt frightened and helpless, and it came out as anger.

qa.q: Why is Simran's letter a better approach than telling Sharmila to cheer up?
qa.a: It apologises, shows concern rather than blame, offers to listen and arranges professional support while respecting Sharmila's choices.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Sharmila may feel relieved and loved, knowing Simran is worried rather than angry and will listen.

grounding: Shows a parent who snapped at a withdrawing child, then approaches with concern, offers to listen and arranges professional support.

passage:
You asked how it was with Darshan last year. I'm Manoj, his father, and I'll be honest, I got it wrong at first.
He was fifteen. He stopped eating dinner with us, stayed in his room, snapped when I asked anything. One night I lost my temper. "What is wrong with you? Just cheer up, you have everything!" He slammed the door.
I sat in the hall feeling useless and angry, mostly at myself.
The next morning I knocked, sat on the edge of his bed and said, "I'm sorry for shouting. I'm worried about you. You don't have to explain everything. I'm just here." He didn't speak for a long time. Then he said, "I feel heavy all the time, Papa."
That week, we saw the school counsellor, and she helped us find a psychologist. He's better now. Slowly. I learned to listen first.

qa.q: What did Manoj shout at Darshan that night?
qa.a: "What is wrong with you? Just cheer up, you have everything!"

qa.q: How did Manoj feel sitting in the hall after the door slammed?
qa.a: He felt useless and angry, mostly at himself.

qa.q: What changed in Manoj's approach, and why did it help?
qa.a: He apologised, showed concern instead of blame, listened without demanding answers and arranged professional support, which let Darshan open up.

qa.q: What was it like for Darshan to hear "Just cheer up"?
qa.a: He probably felt misunderstood and more alone, as if his heavy feeling was his fault.

grounding: Manoj sees his son pull away and snap, feels helpless and angry, and learns that concern, listening and professional support help more than telling him to cheer up.
